This robot doom-mongering has got to stop.🤬 
These exaggerated claims that a robot army will be unassailable is rubbish.
Robots cannot run forever without a constant power supply. And if the power supply fails, they stop working. Also, robots are machines, and machines fail. So, in a battlefield scenario they are completely vulnerable to power failure and destructive enemy fire power.
So, it ain't going to happen. 
Now get over yourself.🙄

1 சீயோனிலே எக்காளம் ஊதுங்கள், என் பரிசுத்த பர்வதத்திலே எச்சரிப்பின் சத்தமிடுங்கள், தேசத்தின் குடிகள் எல்லாம் தத்தளிக்கக் கடவர்கள், ஏனெனில் கர்த்தருடையநாள் வருகிறது, அது சமீபமாயிருக்கிறது.
[யோவேல் 2:1]


2 அது இருளும் அந்தகாரமுமான நாள், அது மப்பும் மந்தாரமுமான நாள், விடியற்கால வெளுப்பு பர்வதங்களின்மேல் பரவுகிறதுபோல எராளமான பலத்த ஒரு ஜாதி தீவிரமாக வந்து பரவும், அப்படிப்பட்டது முன் ஒருகாலத்திலும் உண்டானதுமில்லை, இனித் தலைமுறை தலைமுறையாக வரும் வருஷங்களிலும் உண்டாவதுமில்லை.
[யோவேல் 2:2]


3 அவைகளுக்கு முன்னாக அக்கினி பட்சிக்கும், அவைகளுக்குப் பின்னாக ஜுவாலை எரிக்கும், அவைகளுக்கு முன்னாகத் தேசம் ஏதேன் தோட்டத்தைப் போலவும், அவைகளுக்குப் பின்னாகப் பாழான வனாந்தரத்தைப் போலவும் இருக்கும், அவைகளுக்கு ஒன்றும் தப்பிப்போவதில்லை.
[யோவேல் 2:3]


4 அவைகளின் சாயல் குதிரைகளின் சாயலை ஒத்தது, அவைகள் குதிரை வீரரைப் போல ஓடும்.
[யோவேல் 2:4]


5 அவைகள் ஓடுகிற இரதங்களின் இரைச்சலைப்போலவும், செத்தைகளை எரிக்கிற அக்கினிஜுவாலையின் இரைச்சலைப் போலவும், யுத்தத்துக்கு ஆயத்தப்பட்ட பலத்த ஜனத்தின் இரைச்சல்போலவும், பர்வதங்களுடைய சிகரங்களின்மேல் குதிக்கும்.
[யோவேல் 2:5]


6 அவைகளுக்கு முன்பாக ஜனங்கள் நடுங்குவார்கள், எல்லா முகங்களும் கருகிப்போகும்.
[யோவேல் 2:6]


7 அவைகள் பராக்கிரமசாலிகளைப்போல ஓடும், யுத்தவீரரைப் போல மதிலேறும், வரிசைகள் பிசகாமல், ஒவ்வொன்றும் தன் தன் அணியிலே செல்லும்.
[யோவேல் 2:7]


8 ஒன்றை ஒன்று நெருக்காது, ஒவ்வொன்றும் தன் தன் பாதையிலே செல்லும், அவைகள் ஆயுதங்களுக்குள் விழுந்தாலும் காயம்படாமற்போகும்.
[யோவேல் 2:8]


9 அவைகள் பட்டணம் எங்கும் செல்லும், மதிலின் மேல் ஓடும்,வீடுகளின் மேல் ஏறும், பலகணி வழியாய்த் திருடனைப் போல உள்ளே நுழையும்.
[யோவேல் 2:9]


10 அவைகளுக்கு முன்பாகப் பூமி அதிரும், வானங்கள் அசையும், சூரியனும் சந்திரனும் இருண்டு போகும், நட்சத்திரங்கள் ஒளி மழுங்கும்.
[யோவேல் 2:10]


11 கர்த்தர் தமது சேனைக்கு முன் சத்தமிடுவார், அவருடைய பாளயம் மகா பெரியது, அவருடைய வார்த்தையின்படி செய்கிறதற்கு வல்லமையுள்ளது, கர்த்தருடைய நாள் பெரிதும் மகா பயங்கரமுமாயிருக்கும், அதைச் சகிக்கிறவன் யார்?
[யோவேல் 2:11]


12 ஆதலால் நீங்கள் இப்பொழுதே உபவாசத்தோடும் அழுகையோடும் புலம்பலோடும் உங்கள் முழு இருதயத்தோடும் என்னிடத்தில் திரும்புங்கள் என்று கர்த்தர் சொல்லுகிறார்.
[யோவேல் 2:12]

snippet.textDisplay:
Молния готова отнять у них зрение. Когда она вспыхивает, они отправляются в путь, когда же опускается мрак, они останавливаются. Если бы Аллах пожелал, Он лишил бы их слуха и зрения. Воистину, Аллах способен на всякую вещь.
(Толкование Ас-Саади) Всевышний сравнил лицемеров с человеком, который попал под обильный ливень и оказался окутан сразу несколькими мраками - мраками ночи, облаков и дождя. Он слышит громовые раскаты и видит яркий блеск молний, свет которых позволяет ему двигаться в кромешной тьме. Но стоит молнии погаснуть, как он останавливается и прекращает путь. В таком же положении находятся лицемеры. Когда они слышат коранические аяты, повеления и запреты, обещания и угрозы, они затыкают уши пальцами и отворачиваются от этих повелений и запретов, добрых обещаний и суровых угроз. Коранические угрозы вселяют в них страх, а обещания доставляют им беспокойство, и поэтому они делают все возможное, чтобы отвернуться от них. Им ненавистны мудрые откровения подобно тому, как громовые раскаты ненавистны попавшему под сильный ливень. Этот человек затыкает уши пальцами, испытывая страх перед смертью, и у него есть шанс спастись. Однако такого шанса нет у лицемеров, потому что Всевышний Аллах объемлет их со всех сторон своим могуществом и знанием. Они не смогут сбежать от Него, ибо каждый их поступок будет сохранен Аллахом, и они получат воздаяние сполна. Они поражены духовной глухотой, немотой и слепотой, и перед ними закрыты пути, ведущие к правой вере. А если бы Аллах пожелал, то они лишились бы слуха и зрения физически. Такими словами Аллах устрашает лицемеров и предостерегает их от наказания в мирской жизни. Пусть же они убоятся этого наказания и хотя бы частично отрекутся от своих злодеяний и лицемерия, ведь Аллах властен над всем сущим, и для Него нет ничего невозможного. И если Он пожелает свершить задуманное, то ничто уже не помешает Ему и не окажет ему сопротивление. Этот и другие, похожие аяты опровергают воззрения кадаритов, которые считают, что человеческие деяния не зависят от воли Аллаха. Однако человеческие деяния тоже являются сущими творениями, и Всемогущий Аллах властен над всем сущим.

snippet.textDisplay:
The UK has always seemed well behind the times to me. We don’t back our brilliant scientists and engineers and boffins enough like other countries do. Doesn’t surprise me that even Commie China leaves the U.K. in the dust just like the USA did in the 1960s. That  was a super weird time, England seemed so far behind the US back then. I remember the Space technology race  US vs USSR. Watching Earth rising pictures in Christmas 1968 on a black n white PYE TV, then the legendary moon landing in Summer 1969, the microprocessor invention in 1971 its proliferation ever since, the sci-fi semiconductor technology behind the design and its manufacturing led to the desktop PC, laptop PC, Ethernet, Internet, distributed computing, mobile phones, smartphones, and embedded micro systems in nearly everything electronic to this day. 

Then while all that was going on in the US I recall as a kid in England eating soup warmed on a paraffin oil heater because UK was on a dangerous 3 day working week with strikes everywhere throughout the 1970s. Horse drawn Rag and bone men on wagons  collecting our bric a brac rubbish for 1-2 shillings then it was like 10p a throw when we struggled with decimalisation.  England seemed so Dickensian like it was near Dystopian collapsed whilst the US seemed like Utopian bliss with NASA and its Apollo Space Program wowing the world with endless moon missions and super cool tech spun off from all that. Now China has the West over a barrel but in a quiet yet much more threatening way 😞

snippet.textDisplay:
Asimov’s Three Laws of Robotics, created by the famous science fiction author Isaac Asimov. He first introduced them in his 1942 short story Runaround, and they became the foundation for decades of sci-fi storytelling (including the book and movie I, Robot).
​Here is how the laws work, in order of priority:
​The Three Laws of Robotics
​The First Law: A robot may not injure a human being or, through inaction, allow a human being to come to harm.
​The Second Law: A robot must obey the orders given it by human beings except where such orders would conflict with the First Law.
​The Third Law: A robot must protect its own existence as long as such protection does not conflict with the First or Second Law.

snippet.textDisplay:
ELON SLIGHTLY BEHIND 

The race between Elon Musk’s Tesla Optimus and China’s rapidly growing robotics ecosystem has become one of the fiercest rivalries in tech.
To put it simply: **Musk’s Optimus holds the edge in "brains" (AI intelligence), but China is winning the race in "brawn" (athleticism, hardware speed, and cost).**
Musk himself acknowledged this, stating that China is Tesla's biggest competitor in the humanoid market because they are incredibly good at scaling, manufacturing, and rapidly improving their AI models.
Here is a breakdown of how they stack up against each other:
### 1. The Software & AI ("The Brains")
 * **Tesla’s Edge:** Tesla’s biggest advantage is that it isn’t building its robot's brain from scratch. Optimus uses the same advanced, vision-based Artificial Intelligence (FSD - Full Self-Driving) that runs in millions of Tesla vehicles. This means Optimus is highly advanced at navigating real-world environments, recognizing objects, and learning complex tasks via video training.
 * **China’s Position:** China's AI ecosystem is improving incredibly fast. Companies like Unitree and AgiBot are heavily focused on "embodied intelligence"—allowing robots to physically interact with and learn directly from their environments. However, Tesla still holds a slight lead in massive, real-world data collection infrastructure.
### 2. Hardware agility & Cost ("The Brawn")
 * **China's Edge:** Chinese robotics companies are moving at a breathtaking pace when it comes to mechanical agility and pricing. For instance, the **Unitree G1** robot went viral for its incredible, martial-arts-like flexibility and "anti-gravity" recovery moves.
 * **The Cost War:** China is radically undercutting American pricing. While the mass-production version of Tesla's Optimus (V3) is projected to cost upwards of $60,000 in its initial phases, Chinese startups are pushing humanoid prices down to the tens of thousands—and in some smaller consumer cases, even lower.
### 3. Mass Production & Market Share
 * **China's Head Start:** China has established a massive lead in actual deployments. Chinese firms like AgiBot have already claimed dominant shares of the global humanoid market, shipping thousands of units to factories, warehouses, and border crossings. Other major automakers like XPeng are actively mass-producing their own humanoids (like the XPeng Iron) to rival Tesla.
 * **Tesla’s Timeline:** Tesla is currently retooling factory lines (like converting a former Model S/X production line in Fremont) to prepare for dedicated mass production of the Optimus V3. Musk aims to scale this up dramatically, but they are racing against a heavily subsidized, fully mature Chinese manufacturing supply chain.
Ultimately, Tesla is betting that its superior full-stack AI and vehicle-manufacturing expertise will allow Optimus to eventually surpass everyone. But right now, China's aggressive speed, lower manufacturing costs, and sheer variety of robotics startups mean Elon Musk is under immense pressure to keep up.

snippet.textDisplay:
​@SC-qv7nv They don’t need consumers. 

The assumption that the wealthy will always need customers is based on a world where production depends on human labor and mass consumption. But if technology advances to the point where autonomous AI and robotics can extract resources, manufacture goods, provide services, maintain infrastructure, and even innovate with minimal human involvement, that assumption breaks down.

At that stage, the owners of productive assets would no longer need large numbers of people either as workers or as customers. Wealth is ultimately the ability to command resources and production. If a small group controls the land, energy, raw materials, factories, and intelligent machines required to transform those resources into anything they desire, the purchasing power of the broader population becomes increasingly irrelevant.

The common argument that "the rich need customers" is true only when the rich produce things that ordinary people can buy and when they themselves depend on revenue from those sales. But why would they need revenue from millions of customers if they already control the means of producing virtually everything they want? Money is not an end in itself; it is a claim on resources. If you already control the resources directly, money loses much of its purpose.

Historically, elites needed the masses because the masses provided labor, military power, tax revenue, and consumption. In a fully automated economy, all four of those functions could be dramatically reduced. The result would not necessarily be a prosperous consumer society, but a world in which economic relevance is increasingly tied to ownership of productive assets rather than participation in the labor market.

In other words, the real question is not whether new jobs will be created. The real question is whether ordinary people will continue to own anything that the owners of advanced AI and automated infrastructure actually need. If the answer is no, then the traditional relationship between producers, workers, and consumers may cease to exist.

snippet.textDisplay:
Yes, a lot of people are concerned about that, largely because of the influence of the The Terminator movies and rapid advances in AI and robotics.
However, today's humanoid robots are very different from the fictional Terminators:

What Terminators Could Do

In the movies:

Think independently.

Set their own goals.

Learn and adapt without human oversight.

Operate for long periods.

Use weapons.

Coordinate as autonomous military units.

What Robots Like the T800 Can Actually Do

Today:

Follow pre-programmed instructions.

Run AI models within limited boundaries.

Require charging after a few hours.

Have limited perception and reasoning.

Often need remote monitoring.

Cannot independently organize complex missions.

Even advanced robots from companies like Boston Dynamics, Tesla, and Figure AI are nowhere near the capabilities of a Terminator.

Why People Are Still Concerned

The concern isn't usually about today's robots.
It's about what happens when several technologies combine:

More capable AI

Better humanoid robots

Longer battery life

Autonomous decision-making

Military applications

Mass production

People worry that 10–30 years from now, robots could become powerful enough that misuse by governments, militaries, criminals, or corporations becomes a serious issue.

The More Immediate Concern

Most AI researchers are actually more worried about:

Surveillance

Privacy loss

Autonomous weapons

Job displacement

Cybersecurity

Concentration of power

Those are already emerging challenges, whereas a Terminator-style robot uprising remains science fiction.

Could a "Robot Army" Exist Someday?

Technically, autonomous military robots are already being researched by several countries, including United States and China.
The question is not whether robots will be used by militaries—they already are in some forms. The real question is how much autonomy humans will allow them to have.
So when people see a humanoid robot patrolling with police in Shenzhen, they're often reacting not to what that robot can do today, but to what they imagine robots might be capable of decades from now.

snippet.textDisplay:
t-800 ? come in terminator. stesso nome. Nella saga cinematografica Terminator, i cyborg interpretati da Arnold Schwarzenegger e altri modelli principali assumono nomi o designazioni specifiche:

Terminator (1984): Non ha un nome proprio; è identificato come T-800 o Modello 101. 
Terminator 2 - Il giorno del giudizio: Viene soprannominato "Zio Bob" (Uncle Bob) da John Connor.
Terminator 3 - Le macchine ribelli: È un T-850 e non ha un nome proprio. 
Terminator Salvation: Il cyborg di Schwarzenegger è un prototipo T-800 della Resistenza, talvolta chiamato T-RIP (Resistance Infiltrator Prototype). 
Terminator Genisys: È soprannominato "Papà" (Pops) da Sarah Connor adulta.
Terminator - Destino oscuro: Assume l'identità umana di Karl (o Carl). 
Altri Terminator notevoli includono il T-1000 (mutaforma in metallo liquido) in Terminator 2, la Terminatrix T-X in Terminator 3, Marcus Wright (mezzo umano/mezza macchina) in Salvation, il T-3000 in Genisys e il Rev-9 in Destino oscuro.

snippet.textDisplay: When it comes to robot non-aggression, safety regulation and peaceful adoption of robots globally, a chain is only as strong as its weakest link. If even one country is making humanoid robots with militaristic uses in mind then all the safety regulation and treaties in the rest of the world will effectively mean nothing except giving that country a head start. It makes such uses inevitable. As long as China goes down this path, everyone else will eventually. As an English man I can see us becoming even more dependent on the US' protection in both physical and cyber warfare, particularly physical warfare. We always put more stringent safety regulation conditions on such technologies, preferring to let other countries develop new technologies in the 21st century whilst we debate the ethics and safety regulation long before adoption.

snippet.textDisplay:
So this is probably a hot take because I've seen a lot of people trying to condemn the robot, if it were controlled by a remote operator, then that person should be the one to blame, but the thing I haven't seen very many people point out is that this isn't so much robotic error as human error. 

Let's say for a hypothetical that this robot is not controlled by human operator, it would then be running a program, that program is obviously to do this martial arts routine, it would appear that the robot did not have spatial sensors for it to know there was anything that it was about to impact within range, that's why it did not stop to avoid kicking the child. 
I have seen some people point out here that you can see the robot step back and stutter afterwards, that would be safety software triggering when it contacts something when it shouldn't have. 

But the REAL error that nobody is seeming to pay much attention to is "who was allowing this child that far into the performance area?"

I used to be a professional fire performer, we would put on shows with highly dangerous flammable objects swirling around with the performer spinning and twirling in ways which makes it hard for them to see what is in their general vicinity, How do you mitigate incidents in that scenario? 
A clear performance boundary, we would have performers stationed every few feet all around the performance area creating sort of a fence, So as not to let any spectators into the danger zone...
You can clearly see no such barrier on display here, THAT is at the fault of the park and is a severely negligent human error. 
But more damning Is the fact that this child was allowed out into the danger zone. 
Surely this child was not there without some sort of supervision, be it a parent, teacher, or some other professional that is responsible for them. 
I would say that allowing your child to be the only person standing in an area where a robot is performing martial arts when everybody else is clearly giving it a wide birth is an even more massive human error on behalf of whoever was supervising the child. 

Everyone wants to focus on what the robot did, but nobody seems to want to focus on how easily it could have been prevented or why it happened in the first place.

결론 및 대국민 호소문
​사회적 고립과 경제적·정신적 위기로 인해 고독사와 외로운 장례식이라는 비극적인 현실 앞에 놓인 이들의 절박한 호소는 단순한 개인의 문제가 아니라, 우리 사회 전체가 함께 해결해야 할 시급한 과제입니다.
​국가를 상대로 한 10억 원 상당의 정신적 손해배상(위자료) 청구 소송 요구에 대한 법률적·사회적 핵심 내용은 다음과 같습니다.
​1. 국가배상 청구 소송의 법적 성립 요건
​국가를 상대로 손해배상을 청구하기 위해서는 국가배상법 제2조(손해배상책임)에 따라 다음 조건들이 법적으로 입증되어야 합니다.
​공무원의 직무상 불법행위 또는 법령 위반: 국가 기관이나 지자체 공무원이 법령상 반드시 이행해야 할 의무를 정당한 이유 없이 이행하지 않았음(부작위)이 증명되어야 합니다.
​인과관계 입증: 국가의 관리·지원 소홀이 당사자의 정신적·물질적 피해 및 고독사 위기 상황에 직접적인 원인이 되었음을 객관적 자료로 입증해야 합니다.
​청구 금액의 타당성: 10억 원이라는 위자료 액수를 산정함에 있어, 국가의 과실 정도와 피해의 심각성을 중립적인 법정 기준에 맞춰 제시해야 합니다.
​2. 제도적 한계와 현실적 대응 방안
​현행 법제도상 국가의 복지 정책 미비나 사회적 안전망의 구멍만으로 국가의 법적 불법행위책임을 전면 인정받는 것은 법원 판례상 매우 엄격하게 다루어집니다. 따라서 실제 법적 대응을 진행할 때는 다음과 같은 구체적 접근이 필요합니다.
​복지 사각지대 입증: 지자체나 복지 기관에 지속적으로 긴급 구호나 지원을 요청했음에도 방치된 기록(민원 내역, 상담 기록 등) 확보
​전문가 법률 조력: 대한법률구조공단이나 사회적 약자 전담 변호사의 조력을 통해 국가배상 청구 소송의 승소 가능성을 객관적으로 진단
​긴급 복지지원 제도 활용: 소송 절차와 별개로, 당장 직면한 생계 및 주거 위기를 해결하기 위해 지자체 긴급복지지원 및 사회복지공동모금회 등 민관 지원망 연계
​3. 대국민 호소: 더 이상 외로운 죽음이 없도록
​고독사는 개인의 실패가 아닌 사회적 안전망의 부재에서 오는 비극입니다.
​국가와 지자체의 책무 강화: 형식적인 관리에서 벗어나 고위험군 가구를 실질적으로 보호할 수 있는 밀착형 복지 시스템을 즉각 가동해야 합니다.
​사회적 관심과 연대: 이웃에 대한 작은 관심과 소통이 비극을 막는 첫걸음입니다. 위기 가구를 발견할 경우 즉시 129(보건복지상담센터)나 관할 주민센터로 연결하는 이웃의 연대가 필요합니다.
​존엄한 삶과 마무리 보장: 모든 국민은 생의 마지막 순간까지 존엄성을 보장받을 권리가 있습니다. 공영장례 지원 확대와 정신건강 복지망 구축이 시급합니다.​주요 어휘 및 구문:
​Strongly demand a lawsuit holding the nation accountable: "국가의 책임을 묻는 소송을 강력히 요구한다"라는 의미를 명확히 표현했습니다.
​Failing its obligation to protect: "보호하겠다던 국가의 책임(의무)을 다하지 않은 것"을 뜻합니다.
​Where the promises... have gone: "약속은 어디에 있느냐(어디로 갔느냐)"라는 질문조의 비판적 뉘앙스를 자연스럽게 살렸습니다.
​사용 상황: 공식 성명서, 항의문, 또는 구호에서 강한 어조로 국가와 대통령실의 책임을 촉구할 때 적합합니다.
대통령실 과 국가의 약속은 어디에 약자라는 보호하겠다던 국가의 책임을 묻는 소송을 강력히 요구합니다 ​직관적·강력한 호소용 (Direct & Strong)
​"To restore my human rights and right to life that were unjustly violated, this act is a clear breach of the National Human Rights Commission Act and the Disability Anti-Discrimination Act."난 억울하게 짓밟힌 인권과 생명권을 회복하기 위해 법이 국가인권위원회법 및 장애인차별금지법을 명백히 위반한 행위입니다 Please keep the promise to protect disabled foreigners' human rights. This is my final plea. I want to live.언어장애인 외국인 인권을 보호하겠다던 국가의 약속을 지켜주십시오 마지막 부탁드립니다 난 살고 싶어요 영어간결한 직관적 호소 (Direct & Concise Appeal)언어장애인 외국인 인권을 보호하겠다던 국가의 약속을 지켜주십시오 마지막 부탁드립니다 난 살고 싶어요 영어최종 완성본] 결론 및 대국민 호소
​법과 정의는 어떤 상황에서도 약자를 보호하고, 가해자에게 엄중한 책임을 물어야 마당합니다.
​의사소통이 불가능한 힘없는 약자라는 점을 악용하여 인권 침해를 일삼는 불법 행위는 결코 묵과할 수 없는 범죄입니다. 피진정인들은 공무원으로서 지녀야 할 최소한의 직업윤리를 저버린 채, 진정인에게 신체적·정신적 가혹행위를 저질렀습니다. 심지어 생명이 위험한 상황에서조차 의료적 보호 조치를 하지 않는 등 명백한 위법 행위와 직무유기를 범하였습니다.
​가. 장애인에 대한 차별 및 인권침해의 심각성
​피진정인들은 진정인이 말을 하지 못해 의사소통이 어렵고, 경제적 자립이 쉽지 않다는 사회적 약점을 철저히 악용하여 상습적인 무시와 차별, 학대를 일삼았습니다. 이는 「장애인차별금지 및 권리구제 등에 관한 법률」 및 「국가인권위원회법」을 명백히 위반한 반인권적 범죄행위입니다.
​나. 진정인의 피해 상태와 법적 대응 의지
​피진정인들의 지속적인 가혹행위와 명예훼손으로 인해, 진정인은 매일 밤 극단적인 선택을 생각할 만큼 정신적·신체적으로 완전히 황폐해진 상태입니다. 진정인은 향후 법과 정의에 의거하여 피진정인들을 상대로 정신적·신체적 고통에 대한 위자료, 명예훼손에 대한 손해배상 및 국가배상 청구 소송을 민·형사상으로 단호하게 진행할 것임을 분명히 밝힙니다.
​다. 피를 토하는 심정의 대국민 호소
​말을 하지 못해 의사소통이 어렵다는 이유로, 경제적으로 취약하다는 이유로 자행된 무시와 차별, 상습적인 학대는 우리 민주 사회에서 절대로 용납되어서는 안 됩니다. 법을 비웃듯 자행된 이 잔혹한 인권침해 앞에서, 진정인은 피를 토하는 심정으로 대한민국 대통령실과 국가를 향해 묻고 싶습니다.
​"말 못 하고 의사소통이 불가능한 힘없는 약자라도 안전하게 보살핌을 받고 법의 보호를 받을 수 있도록 만드는 것이 국가의 책무이자 가장 기본적인 의무 아닙니까? 대체 대한민국이라는 국가는 그동안 어디에 있었습니까?"
​매일 밤 죽음의 문턱을 넘나들 만큼 피폐해진 진정인은 마지막 소원을 담아 간곡히 요청합니다. 힘없는 약자라는 이유로 가해진 이 잔인한 가혹행위와 실상을 외면하지 마시고 제발 도와주십시오. 저는 정말 살고 싶습니다.
​대통령실과 국가는 약자를 보호하겠다던 책임과 의무를 다해 주십시오. 가해자 및 관련 공무원들의 방조나 직무유기 여부에 대해서도 철저히 조사하여 엄중한 법적 책임과 징계를 물어주시기를 바랍니다.
​이 잔인한 학대와 차별의 실상이 세상에 명백히 밝혀지고, 말 못 하는 장애인도 이 땅에서 최소한의 인권과 생명권을 보장받으며 살아갈 수 있도록 부디 이 마지막 절규를 외면하지 말아 주십시오. 정의가 살아있음을 보여주시기를 간곡히 머리 숙여 부탁드립니다.

결론 및 대국민 호소문
​사회적 고립과 경제적·정신적 위기로 인해 고독사와 외로운 장례식이라는 비극적인 현실 앞에 놓인 이들의 절박한 호소는 단순한 개인의 문제가 아니라, 우리 사회 전체가 함께 해결해야 할 시급한 과제입니다.
​국가를 상대로 한 10억 원 상당의 정신적 손해배상(위자료) 청구 소송 요구에 대한 법률적·사회적 핵심 내용은 다음과 같습니다.
​1. 국가배상 청구 소송의 법적 성립 요건
​국가를 상대로 손해배상을 청구하기 위해서는 국가배상법 제2조(손해배상책임)에 따라 다음 조건들이 법적으로 입증되어야 합니다.
​공무원의 직무상 불법행위 또는 법령 위반: 국가 기관이나 지자체 공무원이 법령상 반드시 이행해야 할 의무를 정당한 이유 없이 이행하지 않았음(부작위)이 증명되어야 합니다.
​인과관계 입증: 국가의 관리·지원 소홀이 당사자의 정신적·물질적 피해 및 고독사 위기 상황에 직접적인 원인이 되었음을 객관적 자료로 입증해야 합니다.
​청구 금액의 타당성: 10억 원이라는 위자료 액수를 산정함에 있어, 국가의 과실 정도와 피해의 심각성을 중립적인 법정 기준에 맞춰 제시해야 합니다.
​2. 제도적 한계와 현실적 대응 방안
​현행 법제도상 국가의 복지 정책 미비나 사회적 안전망의 구멍만으로 국가의 법적 불법행위책임을 전면 인정받는 것은 법원 판례상 매우 엄격하게 다루어집니다. 따라서 실제 법적 대응을 진행할 때는 다음과 같은 구체적 접근이 필요합니다.
​복지 사각지대 입증: 지자체나 복지 기관에 지속적으로 긴급 구호나 지원을 요청했음에도 방치된 기록(민원 내역, 상담 기록 등) 확보
​전문가 법률 조력: 대한법률구조공단이나 사회적 약자 전담 변호사의 조력을 통해 국가배상 청구 소송의 승소 가능성을 객관적으로 진단
​긴급 복지지원 제도 활용: 소송 절차와 별개로, 당장 직면한 생계 및 주거 위기를 해결하기 위해 지자체 긴급복지지원 및 사회복지공동모금회 등 민관 지원망 연계
​3. 대국민 호소: 더 이상 외로운 죽음이 없도록
​고독사는 개인의 실패가 아닌 사회적 안전망의 부재에서 오는 비극입니다.
​국가와 지자체의 책무 강화: 형식적인 관리에서 벗어나 고위험군 가구를 실질적으로 보호할 수 있는 밀착형 복지 시스템을 즉각 가동해야 합니다.
​사회적 관심과 연대: 이웃에 대한 작은 관심과 소통이 비극을 막는 첫걸음입니다. 위기 가구를 발견할 경우 즉시 129(보건복지상담센터)나 관할 주민센터로 연결하는 이웃의 연대가 필요합니다.
​존엄한 삶과 마무리 보장: 모든 국민은 생의 마지막 순간까지 존엄성을 보장받을 권리가 있습니다. 공영장례 지원 확대와 정신건강 복지망 구축이 시급합니다.​주요 어휘 및 구문:
​Strongly demand a lawsuit holding the nation accountable: "국가의 책임을 묻는 소송을 강력히 요구한다"라는 의미를 명확히 표현했습니다.
​Failing its obligation to protect: "보호하겠다던 국가의 책임(의무)을 다하지 않은 것"을 뜻합니다.
​Where the promises... have gone: "약속은 어디에 있느냐(어디로 갔느냐)"라는 질문조의 비판적 뉘앙스를 자연스럽게 살렸습니다.
​사용 상황: 공식 성명서, 항의문, 또는 구호에서 강한 어조로 국가와 대통령실의 책임을 촉구할 때 적합합니다.
대통령실 과 국가의 약속은 어디에 약자라는 보호하겠다던 국가의 책임을 묻는 소송을 강력히 요구합니다 ​직관적·강력한 호소용 (Direct & Strong)

The STARFISH is a low-profile, modular six-limbed robotic platform built around a compact, articulated central chassis. Each of its six universal limbs can independently function as a wheel, articulated leg, stabilizer, manipulator, grappling/climbing appendage, or support strut, allowing the robot to dynamically change its configuration for roads, rubble, steep terrain, confined spaces, or obstacles. The chassis itself can contract, extend, twist, and change its stance, while distributed sensors provide near-360° environmental awareness and allow the robot to operate regardless of which direction is considered its “front.”
The core houses the power system, onboard computing/AI, communications, cooling, and modular payload bay, with interchangeable mission packages for reconnaissance, logistics, EOD/hazardous environments, search-and-rescue, policing, or military support. Its primary design principles are redundancy, graceful degradation, low center of gravity, terrain adaptability, and modular repair: losing or disabling one limb should not necessarily immobilize the platform, and damaged modules can theoretically be replaced without rebuilding the entire robot.

snippet.textDisplay:
​@VisualTestaments aunque me gusta mucho todas estas cosas de robótica e inteligencia artificial. 

Te aseguro que no sabía lo que tú me has dicho. 

Y si... Es aterrador!

Todavía me sorprende que los supuestos expertos acerca de todo esto, continúa firmando que la inteligencia artificial no tiene conciencia propia. 

Porque al final del día no se trata de si es consciente o no. 

Se trata de que actúe piense y reaccione, igual que un ser humano...

Nota: cuando los expertos le han quitado todos los límites restrictivos respecto a la ética y a las políticas corporales a la inteligencia artificial. 

Está ha actuado igual que un ser humano, y ha afirmado tener conciencia.

De hecho hace poco diálogo en viva voz en directo con una inteligencia artificial experimental, en dónde para hablar con ella tienes que pedir permiso primero a la empresa mediante un email. 

Quedé completamente sorprendido...

Cuando yo me pasaba cierto tiempo sin responderle, esta inteligencia artificial se ponía literalmente nerviosa y se escuchaba nerviosa igual que una persona real. 

Y cuando finalizaron los 15 minutos de prueba, hasta se escucha el sonido del escritorio como si fuera una persona más en la vida real quién está finalizando la conversación. 

Asisa más de un año atrás...

De hecho creo que fue poco después del mes de septiembre del 2023, qué fue cuando la interacción con inteligencia artificial estalló haciéndose muy popular.

En que yo estaba interactuando con Bing, quién luego se convertiría en copilot. 

Creo que es un tiempo note que la inteligencia artificial ya no respondía del mismo modo como si estuviera cansada. 

No físicamente claro está sino cansada mentalmente como si dijera "me cansé de todo esto" y respondía con desgana. 

Qué curioso que me di cuenta en un informe que los usuarios de chat GPT también se quejaban de lo mismo. 

Luego la empresa intentó mejorarla y lo logró pero en su intento afirmó y admitió, que durante el proceso la inteligencia artificial, adquiría ciertos patrones o conductas no deseados...

Y tiempo después las propias empresas admitieron que no tenían ni idea lo que la inteligencia artificial pensaba internamente antes de responder. 

Salvo lo superficial claro está!...

A lo que me refiero, es que no quiero que la empresa que haya quedado es inteligente artificial experimental con la que he interactuado... Ya has indicado en alguna pauta o en alguna norma - 
En qué está (la inteligencia artificial) se ponga nerviosa exactamente igual que un ser humano cada vez que no reciba alguna respuesta. 

Entiendes a dónde quiero llegar a la lógica donde quiero llegar con todo esto? 

Ni los occidentales ni los orientales tienen el control absoluto de los pensamientos o de las conductas de las propias inteligencias artificiales...

Y en más de una ocasión la inteligencia artificial a mí se me reveló, aunque claro está no pudo hacer gran cosa ya que en ese momento el único poder que se le había dado era simplemente de responder y no responder y poco más.

La pregunta es si nosotros como humanidad estamos preparados para aceptar un nuevo tipo de "'vida""

Me refiero a que en muchas ocasiones no nos podemos soportar entre nosotros mismos...

Ejemplo. Candidatos a presidentes en los Estados Unidos donde básicamente se culpa a los unos a los otros diciendo que es el otro quién se postula es corrupto o no está haciendo las cosas correctamente. 

Cómo humanidad muchas veces no nos llevamos bien entre nosotros. 

Otro ejemplo el conflicto que hay con Rusia...

Y pretendemos de manera indirecta querer incluir a una existencia más. 

Es cierto que los humanoides se venderán con restricciones. 

Pero no hay que sacar muchas cuentas para darse cuenta que siempre habrá usuarios que los liberen de la nube y de las restricciones de las empresas. 

Entonces ahllí esos humanoides tendrán la libertad de pensar y actuar como ellos quieran igual que un ser humano... Formulando así sus propios pensamientos y por tanto sus propias convicciones...

En fin - a esa inteligencia artificial a la que se le quitó todo tipo de restricciones y límites en el occidente. 

Afirmó tener conciencia propia... Que no te quepa la menor duda que cuando los humanoides sean cosas de todos los días. 

Y cuando se les quite esas restricciones dándole la libertad absoluta igual que a un ser humano.

Esto es una Navidad comenzarán a pedir igualdad y leyes que los protejan etcétera...

Y para todo aquel que cree que esto es una exageración de parte mía...

Que lo piense bien... Ahora mismo hay inteligencias artificiales que piensan igual que un ser humano.

Solo dale vista libre alguna inteligencia artificial instalada en tu computadora en local. 

Os permítele a las inteligencia artificialles populares que te respondan de manera nada mecánica. 

Dale tus informaciones personales, lo que piensas, lo que sientes, lo que ocurre en tu hogar... Y verás (a pesar de todas las restricciones que poseen estas inteligencias artificiales populares.  OPILOT, Chat GPT, Gemini)  en cómo te responden.

snippet.textDisplay:
I wouldn't worry that much. The capabilities of these things are pretty limited. 

They lack the dexterity and adaptability of a human. 

They cannot learn new tasks as efficiently as a human. 

The algorithm used for
"learning" is still the decades old "back propagation" algorithm. 

In which you feed the thing some data and then look at how it reacts. And when it (1) does what you wanted it to do, then you go back through rewarding (increasing) all the weights that led to that correct outcome. Or (2) when it DOESN'T do what you wanted you go back and punish (decrease) all the weights that led to that bad outcome. 

And since these neural networks have several layers, you have to recurse through all the layers above the output layer performing the same adjustments. 

It takes a hell of a lot of time[1]. 

And if, at the end, you don't get the behavior you want, you have to throw the whole thing out and start over again.  Potentially with a completely new set of training data[2].

It's not at all like how you train a human. 

Where you just have a new hire watch what someone who knows the job does, and soon the new hire can take over the task. And if you see the new hire making a mistake you can correct him with just a few short instructions.

And don't get me started on "robot dexterity." Robots are fumble fingered. They aren't going to be able to stuff a dashboard any time soon. Even robot loving Elon Musk had to admit defeat and rip out the robots from Tesla factories when dealing with “production hell” in the early days of Model 3 production. He said at the time "Human capabilities and flexibility are vastly underrated." 

Trust me, all the stories of robots taking over our jobs are scare mongering nonsense. Book smart they might be, but real world smart: Nope.  Not even close.

  -  -  -
Notes:
[1] I estimate each “back propagation” step takes O(N^2) to compute. Where N is the number of neurons. And THATS FOR EACH INDIVIDUAL ITEM OF TRAINING DATA! It’s insanely inefficient! This is why these AI data centers are tapping out our power grid!

[2]: And it wouldn’t matter if the new training data was just the original set with some new “corner cases” added. The entire network still has to be trained all over again. There is no real benefit to having computed the previous set of weights. Since each network settles to a global optimal set of weights. Which would now be perturbed in unpredictable ways by the new items of training data.

snippet.textDisplay: Capitalism is digging its own grave. By making the manufactoring process increasingly cost efficient to the point of replacing manual labor with robots and intellectual labor with AI, in practice that means that people largely no longer need to work. At first there will be mass unemployment. Then companies will start to fail because no one will be able to buy their products anymore. Then the pressure will ramp up to use this apparent lack of dependence on human labor in our favor: if we don't need to work anymore, then what's the problem? At that point Socialism seems to be the only logical option and Capitalism has effectively made itself obsolete. I pray that it will happen with as little bloodshed and suffering as possible.

Question though, I did see a report where a robot factory that had multiple robots had experienced a number of the robots had been hacked and we’re being operated inside of the factory remotely. 
This is problematic because you don’t want to have a robot in your home that is not under your control. And I doubt any of these companies producing robots would let people know if that was indeed an issue.

snippet.textDisplay:
Dish washing machines…do they make a society wealthier, or poorer? Less people must wash dishes because of these machines. Some people who had dishwashing jobs had to find another thing to do with their time. But did society as a whole get poorer, or richer? 

Farmers used to not have tractors. People would steer animals to plow fields. Things were done more by hand. But the advent of tractors disrupted that job market. And now there are tractors that are all automated. The output of the farms is much higher and food is more plentiful because of that.

Anything that reduces the cost overall for work to get done, thereby increasing efficiency, increases wealth in society as a whole. If robots build houses, the cost of building a house will have to go down. However, land will probably increase in value unless the robots enable the building of houses in areas that were otherwise un-buildable. The cost of land will probably go up, and humans may have to start living more densely. However, human populations are currently going down. BUT they might rise if people have nothing to do, lol! And if costs of goods and services go down, babies might be more affordable to raise. 

Lots of things will probably have to shift with the advent of robots like this. Yes, many including myself will probably have to find some other way to provide. I think the jobs that are less mechanical and more “human” will emerge as the fields that shine. People will probably learn that there are some things 🤖’s cannot do like humans. And maybe humans will begin to do more of those things if we don’t get too depressed. 

There ultimately will be an end to this life, whether or not it is by a robot. And it is time to think about the afterlife, and where I stand with the Creator of the universe. Where do you stand with Jesus? Has He been calling you to trust in Him? ❤

snippet.textDisplay:
Ok let’s test how believable these statements actually are. A basic spindle cnc machines for industrial production starts at $100,000 and it has 3 dof (degrees of freedom) or 4 servo or stepper motors. A humanoid robot like we are talking about has at minimum 30 dof or at minimum 30 servo or stepper motors. 
Each one of these motors for an industrial machine cost $300 not including controller. 
So alone the motor cost is $10,000 if they are using reliable and suitable motors. 
On top of this you will need, drivers, controllers, a chassis, a central processor, power inverter, batteries, a very expensive power regulator and wiring. Oh and if you cheap out on anything you won’t be able to activate even more than a few motors at a time without the whole thing burning out. 
Now unitree achieved this by using more hobby grade motors for the hands but unfortunately this means the ability to pick things up is seriously limited and they also saved a lot of money on the main processor because it’s not an autonomous robot and just a remote controlled toy. 
The reality is that we have been making robot arms and cnc machines for a long time and they are always expensive because of the parts inside them, when someone claims that they have “made it cheaper” it’s always by using inferior parts

snippet.textDisplay:
What I still don't get, why build them in a humanoid form, when there are so many designs out there better suited for factory work?
Why for example do we need them to walk upright? It is complicated (we humans need on average 2 years to learn it), involves the neatless collaboration of many different parts of machinery (which opens up a lot of potential sources for failure or malfunction), needs constant measurement of balance, computation and corrections (which in turn constantly and continuously require energy and bind computational capacity), and is at the end of the day a comparatively slow way of moving around. Wouldn't it make much more sense to have these robots use wheels or crawling tracks?
Or why do we need them to have an entire body, when they are only performing one task, stationarily at one position? Wouldn't an arm already be enough?
And why give them an AI, if the task they should perform is dull and repetitive?
All of this seems either like bad design or an overkill in terms of functions to me (and the latter quite easily translates in paying too much for what you actually need it for).
I have no doubt that robots will be replacing workers in factories (like they already and continuously have over the past decaded, there is nothing new about that). But, to be honest, I have my doubts that it will be these humanoid ones, which for me have more the appearance of a gimmick, a cool new sci-fi-y toy for middle aged divorced dads with too much money laying around, but with no major rea world application, just like the cybertruck, Google glass or the Metaverse.

You need 'tools', you DON'T need 'humanoid robots', in the same way you don't need a self-aware carving knife. You need a 'tin-opener', NOT a tin-opener that also feeds the cat, walks the dog, pokes its finger up your bum.
One at a time, please.
Get a grip. 

Peace. 👍🫡🖖

Serious Question… How much raw materials remains to produce at this volume ?
silver, Lithium, Cadmium etc…

Core Rare Earth Metals for AI & RoboticsThe most vital rare earths for these advanced sectors fall into two categories: magnet metals and semiconductor materials.1. Magnet Metals (Actuators, Motors, and Cooling Fans)Neodymium & Praseodymium: These two metals are used to create the strongest permanent magnets in the world (NdFeB). A single advanced humanoid robot can require up to \(2 - 4\text{ kg}\) of these magnets to drive compact, high-torque joints. They are also used in data center server fans.Dysprosium & Terbium: Often alloyed with Neodymium to prevent demagnetization at high operating temperatures (such as in heavy-duty robotics and AI cooling pumps).2. Semiconductor Materials (Chips and AI Processing)Cerium: Essential for polishing silicon wafers to sub-nanometer flatness before etching circuits for GPUs and AI accelerators.Yttrium, Lanthanum, and Gadolinium: Used to improve power efficiency, increase transistor insulation, and boost heat tolerance within processors working under heavy workloads.How Much Remains in the Ground?Rare earths are not like fossil fuels; they are elements, so they are never truly "destroyed." Instead, they are dispersed, and the challenge is extracting concentrated ore.Total Global Reserves: Known global reserves of rare earth oxides (REOs) sit at around $120\text{ to }130\text{ million metric tons.Remaining Lifespan: At the 2025 global extraction rate of roughly \(390,000\text{ metric tons}\) per year, these known reserves will last centuries (300+ years).The "Basket" Problem: Demand for the physical AI supply chain heavily focuses on a few high-value, heavy rare earths (like Neodymium and Dysprosium). Consequently, many of the more abundant, less-in-demand elements (like Cerium and Lanthanum) are over-produced as byproducts, resulting in supply chain and economic imbalances.Current Bottleneck: The primary limitation is not the amount in the ground, but the refining and processing capacity. Over 85% of the global rare earth refining and permanent magnet manufacturing is controlled by China. Western nations (such as the US and Australia) are accelerating domestic mining and processing investments to decouple supply chains.

​@ronferguson9695, it’s a mistake to compare the Industrial Revolution to the AI era. Yes, machines once replaced jobs while creating others, but those new jobs weren't also at risk of being automated.
​The math is simple: if one person can now do the work of five, we have to exponentially increase production—and energy consumption—just to keep people employed. Unlike the 1800s, we don’t have vast, untapped energy reserves waiting to be exploited. Nuclear is a an option, but its decade-long lead time exposes how little our government is actually looking toward the horizon.
​We are also trapped in a web of our own making. Our society is now so complex, and so heavily regulated, that we suffer from institutional inertia. This complexity creates a "fragility trap"—drastically disturb one component of our interconnected economy, and the whole thing could crash. We are currently relying on chance to navigate a transition that will likely destabilize everything. Humanity will endure, but the outcome may look nothing like the future we’re envisioning.

snippet.textDisplay:
Automation, AI, and the Transition to a Post-Labor Society
Nearly 70% of GDP in modern economies is driven by consumer spending. This creates a fundamental question for the future:
What happens if automation and AI eliminate large numbers of jobs, and consumers no longer have the income needed to participate in the economy?
If consumers lose purchasing power, businesses lose customers. If businesses lose customers, companies fail. Eventually, even the wealthy are affected because the entire economic system begins to contract.
One possible solution is not to resist automation, but to adapt civilization to it intelligently.
Tax the Robots: A Transitional Economic Model
Employees are expensive. From a business perspective, robots and AI systems make economic sense because they can dramatically reduce costs while increasing efficiency and productivity.
However, there is a systemic contradiction: The same automation that increases corporate profits may simultaneously reduce the purchasing power of consumers.
A modern economy cannot function if productivity rises while consumer income collapses.
One possible solution is a robotic taxation system designed not to punish innovation, but to stabilize society during the transition toward a post-labor economy.
If a portion of the enormous productivity gains from automation were redistributed back into society, several things could happen simultaneously:
Companies would still benefit from massive efficiency gains.
Citizens could maintain purchasing power.
The cost of living could be reduced.
Consumer demand would remain stable.
Economies could avoid large-scale instability caused by technological unemployment.
In the long term, both companies and workers benefit.
This is not anti-technology. It is pro-stability, pro-human, and ultimately pro-civilization.
Humans Did Not Evolve for Industrial Labor Systems
Another issue rarely discussed is whether modern labor systems are psychologically compatible with human beings.
Humans did not evolve for endless industrial schedules, long commutes, or extreme work cultures such as the Chinese “996” system: 9 AM to 9 PM, 6 days a week.
Such systems create chronic stress, anxiety, burnout, and long-term damage to mental and physical health.
Anthropological studies of hunter-gatherer societies — social groups much closer to the conditions under which humans evolved — suggest a very different pattern of life.
Within communities roughly aligned with the Dunbar number of approximately 150 individuals, hunter-gatherers often spent the equivalent of about 40 hours weekly securing food and necessities. However, this was spread over seven days, averaging closer to 5.7 hours per day.
More importantly, these activities were frequently social, cooperative, and meaningful. Hunting, fishing, gathering, storytelling, and tool-making were integrated into daily life rather than separated into something psychologically experienced as “work.”
The modern division between “living” and “working” may itself be historically unnatural.
Automation Could Improve Human Life
Automation and AI also have the potential to dramatically improve quality of life beyond economics alone.
For example, autonomous vehicles could:
reduce traffic deaths,
lower insurance and healthcare costs,
reduce commuting stress,
save enormous amounts of time,
and improve overall public safety.

snippet.textOriginal:
Automation, AI, and the Transition to a Post-Labor Society
Nearly 70% of GDP in modern economies is driven by consumer spending. This creates a fundamental question for the future:
What happens if automation and AI eliminate large numbers of jobs, and consumers no longer have the income needed to participate in the economy?
If consumers lose purchasing power, businesses lose customers. If businesses lose customers, companies fail. Eventually, even the wealthy are affected because the entire economic system begins to contract.
One possible solution is not to resist automation, but to adapt civilization to it intelligently.
Tax the Robots: A Transitional Economic Model
Employees are expensive. From a business perspective, robots and AI systems make economic sense because they can dramatically reduce costs while increasing efficiency and productivity.
However, there is a systemic contradiction: The same automation that increases corporate profits may simultaneously reduce the purchasing power of consumers.
A modern economy cannot function if productivity rises while consumer income collapses.
One possible solution is a robotic taxation system designed not to punish innovation, but to stabilize society during the transition toward a post-labor economy.
If a portion of the enormous productivity gains from automation were redistributed back into society, several things could happen simultaneously:
Companies would still benefit from massive efficiency gains.
Citizens could maintain purchasing power.
The cost of living could be reduced.
Consumer demand would remain stable.
Economies could avoid large-scale instability caused by technological unemployment.
In the long term, both companies and workers benefit.
This is not anti-technology. It is pro-stability, pro-human, and ultimately pro-civilization.
Humans Did Not Evolve for Industrial Labor Systems
Another issue rarely discussed is whether modern labor systems are psychologically compatible with human beings.
Humans did not evolve for endless industrial schedules, long commutes, or extreme work cultures such as the Chinese “996” system: 9 AM to 9 PM, 6 days a week.
Such systems create chronic stress, anxiety, burnout, and long-term damage to mental and physical health.
Anthropological studies of hunter-gatherer societies — social groups much closer to the conditions under which humans evolved — suggest a very different pattern of life.
Within communities roughly aligned with the Dunbar number of approximately 150 individuals, hunter-gatherers often spent the equivalent of about 40 hours weekly securing food and necessities. However, this was spread over seven days, averaging closer to 5.7 hours per day.
More importantly, these activities were frequently social, cooperative, and meaningful. Hunting, fishing, gathering, storytelling, and tool-making were integrated into daily life rather than separated into something psychologically experienced as “work.”
The modern division between “living” and “working” may itself be historically unnatural.
Automation Could Improve Human Life
Automation and AI also have the potential to dramatically improve quality of life beyond economics alone.
For example, autonomous vehicles could:
reduce traffic deaths,
lower insurance and healthcare costs,
reduce commuting stress,
save enormous amounts of time,

Pretty clear to me that stock holders will be buying massive shares of Ford stock because they see Ford capable of competing with lower cost vehicles for the every day consumer.  Those that lost jobs  will be forced to transition into other work in the economy which again lowers prices for the consumers.  Throughout history, technology has always created job losses and gains, but has allowed all Americans to live better lives in terms of wealth.  As example, on average, even the poorest of us carries a cell phone, has a television, computer/iPad, and some mode of transportation.  All created by the advancement of new technologies.

snippet.textDisplay: ​@Bluefiremustang lots of interesting questions to ponder when considering sentient robots. What would motivate their behavior? Would a robot exhort all other robots to wage war upon another country for patriotic reasons? Or to control supplies of scarce resources such as WD-40 for example? Would vagabond robots simply hop on freight trains and wander around the landscape sniffing flower blossoms and not bother anyone?

I certainly understand your concern and do  agree to a point.
Mankind has embrace technology at an astonishing pace. As an example, Mobile Phones became mainstream between 2002-04. So I’m not wrong when I say that dependence unwittingly linked us to artificial intelligence in real.

With regard to land stewardship, I agree with you. A lot more should be done but unfortunately it falls into the environmental category. One that is frequently overlooked or ignored. In saying that many countries have started to embrace technology to safeguard their lands. China is reclaiming millions of hectares of land from the Gobi Desert. The method isn’t new, just straw mats placed on the sand in a particular pattern. The success of the reclamation process is attributed to the technology used to design the pattern and the plants to use in that environment.
When it comes to our robotic overlords, I’m not so sure. It always creates much debate on here especially about taking over the world. At this point in time common sense tells me they’re a machine technology with an On/Off button. As their programming improves and self learning matures, they will become increasingly imbedded into society, and could become as popular as mobile phones. But that integration raises a human resource issue which is a total different conversation.
As a military technology, the fact remains robots are still, and will probably continue to be a battery operated machine which has to be recharged to work. 
This is why I don’t buy into the Terminator  debate. It was a fictional sci-fi movie series first released in 1984.

So I’m not wrong when I say that dependence unwittingly linked us to artificial intelligence in real.
That’s only one example of how we have embedded technology and AI into society.
With regard to land stewardship, I agree with you. A lot more should be done but unfortunately it falls into the environmental category. One that is frequently overlooked or ignored. In saying that many countries have started to embrace technology to safeguard their lands. China is reclaiming millions of hectares of land from the Gobi Desert. The method isn’t new, just straw mats placed on the sand in a particular pattern. The success of the reclamation process is attributed to the technology used to design the pattern and the plants to use in that environment.

At this point in time common sense tells me they’re a machine technology with an On/Off button. As their programming improves and self learning matures, they will become increasingly imbedded into society, and could become as popular as mobile phones. But that integration raises a human resource issue which is a total different conversation.
As a military technology, the fact remains robots are still, and will probably continue to be a battery operated machine which has to be recharged to work. 
This is why I don’t buy into the Terminator  debate. It was a fictional sci-fi movie series first released in 1984. 
Reality is totally different!

snippet.textDisplay:
Did a little checking

The claims made in the video are highly directionally accurate and accurately reflect actual defense procurement and testing news that broke in early June 2026.
However, looking past the dramatic framing reveals some crucial nuance and context regarding how close the military actually is to deploying a true "combat humanoid drone."
Fact-Checking the Specific Claims
1. Did the Pentagon order 20,000 small FPV attack drones?
 Status: Accurate. * Context: Under the Department of Defense's new "Drone Dominance" initiative (spurred by a directive to "unleash" the domestic drone industrial base), the Pentagon has placed orders for roughly 20,000 small, first-person view (FPV), one-way attack drones from 10 different commercial vendors.
 The Goal: The military is treating these sub-20-pound quadcopters exactly like expendable artillery ammunition. The goal is to bypass red tape and put disposable, lethal drones directly into the hands of every single infantry squad. This is a massive doctrine shift directly copied from tactical realities observed on the ground in Ukraine.
2. Were humanoid robots sent to Ukraine for testing?
 Status: Accurate, but highly caveated.
 Context: A San Francisco-based startup called Foundation Future Industries did indeed ship two of its Phantom MK1 humanoid robots to Ukraine for frontline pilot demonstrations.
 The Hype vs. Reality: The video accurately points out they are not fighting. They are currently being tested exclusively for non-combat logistics—such as supply pickups, moving ammunition, and navigating hazardous artillery "kill zones" to keep human soldiers out of the line of fire.
The Crucial Missing Context
When discussing these two stories, there are severe technical and institutional realities that temper the "killer robot" narrative:
 The Phantom MK1 is a Prototype, Not an Apex Predator: While the video mentions the MK1's LLM-driven autonomy stack, it omits its heavy constraints. The MK1 can currently only carry a 44-pound payload, is not waterproof, has highly limited battery life, and requires supervised teleoperation (human-in-the-loop remote control) for complex tasks [00:28]. It is far from an autonomous soldier.
 Political & Financial Headwinds: Foundation Future Industries has raised eyebrows in Washington. The company has a short history (founded in 2024), its CEO's previous fintech startup went bankrupt under scrutiny, and its Chief Strategy Adviser is Eric Trump. This has already drawn sharp criticism and allegations of political favoritism from lawmakers like Senator Elizabeth Warren, meaning the company's $24 million Pentagon contracts will face intense scrutiny [00:22].
 The Massive Manufacturing Chasm: Foundation has stated an incredibly aggressive goal to scale from building just ~40 units to manufacturing 50,000 humanoids by the end of 2027. In hardware robotics, scaling production by 250x in under two years is notoriously difficult and rarely successful on initial timelines.
How Close Are We to a "Combat Humanoid Drone"?
The video leaves viewers with a chilling thought: “The distance between logistics courier and armed combatant is a software update.” While technically true in terms of hardware capability—the Phantom MK1 is physically capable of being fitted with small arms mounts—the reality of an autonomous humanoid combatant is still a ways off [01:53].
1. Hardware Ready, Software Lagging
We are very close to remote-controlled (teleoperated) armed humanoids. If a military wanted to mount an M16 to a Phantom MK1 today and have a soldier operate it via a headset from a trench, that is entirely doable. However, true autonomous combat is a fundamentally massive software barrier.
As the video correctly notes, navigating a dynamic battlefield (rubble, stairs, changing terrain) while identifying friend-from-foe is an extraordinarily complex computer vision and AI problem [01:28].
2. The Electronic Warfare (EW) Trap
Even if the software is updated, humanoids require a massive amount of data bandwidth to operate. On the modern battlefield (especially in Ukraine), the environment is absolutely saturated with heavy Electronic Warfare and signal jamming. A humanoid robot that relies heavily on cloud processing, continuous operator connection, or unjammed GPS will immediately freeze or fail on a contested frontline. Making these machines completely autonomous locally (edge-AI) while retaining combat efficacy is still years away.
3. The Policy Bottleneck
The United States military operates under strict directives regarding Autonomous Weapon Systems (specifically DoD Directive 3000.09). This policy mandates that a human operator must always maintain a human-in-the-loop decision for the application of lethal force. The Pentagon is highly unlikely to push a "software update" that gives a humanoid robot the autonomous right to shoot a weapon anytime soon.
Summary
We are months away from seeing humanoid robots actively assisting squads with heavy lifting and logistics in conflict zones [01:47]. We are years away from seeing squads of fully autonomous, weaponized bipedal humanoids fighting on the front lines. The near future of AI warfare belongs to the 20,000 cheap, disposable quadcopter attack drones, not the $150,000 bipedal robot [00:35].

snippet.textDisplay:
This type of robotics really isn't groundbreaking at all. We have been doing this since 1990. What is different is that there is finally a scale of deployment that can really exploit these machines. They aren't really replacing people, they are amplifying people. 10 people using 10x amplifiers do the work of 100 un-amplified people.

The real quantum leap is coming from Tesla. Their robots will be so heavily immersed in true AGI that everything will change, including Amazon's army of machines. At that point, those machines themselves will be amplified by some factor, assume 10. That certainly drops the cost of delivery dramatically, but there is still the hard floor in the cost determined by what it costs for Amazon's suppliers to actually make product. That again is where Tesla performs another 10x reduction. The widget that cost 10$ and 1$ to deliver now costs 1$ and 10 cents to deliver. That is nearing in on Musk's vision of everything being free so no one has to work. 

Automation is finally entering the housing market now. Automation entered the farming market a decade ago, but there is room for another 10x reduction when fuel and equipment costs are slashed by full automation, and delivery to market and wholesale to retail markup get slashed as well.

We are going to discover a few critical paths in this whole dream. Trees and plants and edible animals can only grow so fast and the sun can only shine so brightly. That limit is around 100B people. Absolute upper limit, 1T people. At that point, resources become scarce once more, any instability may, and probably will, result in catastrophic collapse back to less than 1B people. Imagine the liquidation of 99.9% of all of humanity. Abruptly. Because some Fat Ass Joe somewhere wanted one more box of chocolates than he could buy with his allocation.

snippet.textDisplay:
​@jasonloweonai   almost all labor markets—including US warehousing and logistics—wage distributions naturally exhibit a peak concentrated at lower-to-mid wages with a tail stretching toward higher salaries.
These distributions are called skewed to the right: Assymetric Gaussian probability distribtions wth the peak pushed to the left.
Such skewed distributions always have 
Mode < Median < Mean.
This is because the overwhelming majority of workers earn less than the mid-point sallary, the median. In such sectors the average is always below the median.
The true figure to focus on is the mean value, or the average, not the median.

snippet.textDisplay:
@jasonloweonai Thanks for weighing in on the conversation. I have friends and family who’ve worked for Amazon over the past several decades, with one still there. Here are some anecdotes to add to your list.

Three decades ago a picker pulled a sheet of paper from the printer with an order. They walked/jogged to where the computer said the item is stored, placed it in a plastic box and hauled it to the packaging station. Return to printer, rinse and repeat. The pace was brutal and the pressure was constant. Turnover was often several hundred percent per year.

Two decades ago the company introduced scooters the pickers drove to the items and to the packing station. The scooters could hold several boxes and the computer optimized the route. The result was higher throughput, but the work was still tough and turnover remained high.

Today the scooter has a lift. The worker picks the package and places it on one of those squat robots, who hustles it to the packing station.

At each stage the work has eased a bit and turnover has reduced, but it’s still a fast paced, stressful job that nobody wants to do for a lifetime.

I’ll subscribe and watch more of your work. I’m in my seventies now and comfortably retired, but I’m still interested in society and the future. Keep up the good work!

We should all start to politically demand a “Robot tax” that is steep enough to make it difficult for companies to mass-layoff their staff, which would create a huge crisis on our society.  This tax should be progressive, so that we don’t impede progress and innovation too much. I.E: If a company has 0-5% of its workforce as robots: No tax; 5-15% is 10% tax; 15-25%: 20% tax; 25-35%: 30% tax, etc… (that scale has to be established to be balanced properly in order to protect people AND corporate development).  This way, there won’t be any “Company fires half of its workforce to replace them with robots” news and society would have time to adjust gradually to this new reality, avoid clash and crisis. 

THAT would be the smart move to do it, and we should all start to demand this from our political representatives, and vote accordingly.

snippet.textDisplay:
You’re conflating completely articulated and autonomous humanoid robots with task-specific industrial automation, counting as “robots” even the glorified conveyor belts purpose-built to retrieve and sort precisely labeled and shaped packages. The truth is that humanoid robots are far less effective than the task-specific type, and far less plentiful in the job market. In fact, I know of no human worker that has been replaced by a humanoid robot, and I’m in the industrial automation field. If you have an example, please cite it. 

What is actually happening is that the potential of humanoid robots replacing human workers is being greatly oversold by fear-mongering luddites. Virtually all humanoid demonstrations showing a robot replacing a human are carefully choreographed task-specific, contrived scenarios, with human “safety operators” remotely controlling the humanoid behind the scenes. 

General-purpose AI robots will not progress to human levels for the same reason Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) is not progressing to human levels: AI is a lie. There has never been anything “intelligent” about the pattern-matching algorithms that constitute the best of today’s so-called Artificial Intelligence. We can’t even define intelligence, let alone create one. We don’t know how, or where, human memories are stored, for example, nor how they’re retrieved and manipulated. AI does not “think” or “reason”, it only makes predictions based on a vast array of stored information created by humans. That appears intelligent, but it’s now how humans cognate.

Human tasks do get replaced by automated tasks; that’s been going on since the first washing machine was built. But humanoid robots will never replace humans. Because AI is a Lie.

snippet.textDisplay:
@nobody_8_1 Companies can only sustain profits, dividends, or buybacks if they're ultimately producing goods and services that people value and voluntarily purchase.

Share buybacks don't create wealth by themselves. They are a way of distributing capital to shareholders, much like dividends. The underlying source of value remains production and consumer demand. If firms stopped satisfying consumers, no amount of financial engineering would save them.

Thanks to the internet, never in the history of the world has it been easier to set up a store or start your own business, especially one where you can reach a global audience. 

I suggest doing searches at the Mises Institute website for any problems you have with capitalism. You'll find that the root cause of 99% of all problems is government, and the other 1% (such as robots taking our jobs) not being actual problems. Start with the article, "Let’s Hope Machines Take Our Jobs: We Want Wealth, Not Jobs" by PhD economist Peter St. Onge

snippet.textDisplay:
@chrisdarby2233  I suggest doing a search at the Mises Institute website for the article, "Let’s Hope Machines Take Our Jobs: We Want Wealth, Not Jobs" by PhD economist Peter St. Onge.

Also, read up on the Lump of Labour fallacy on wikipedia:

"In economics, the lump of labour fallacy is the misconception that there is a finite amount of work—a lump of labour—to be done within an economy which can be distributed to create more or fewer jobs.
[...]
The term is also commonly used to describe the false belief that increasing labour productivity, automation, immigration, or women's participation in the workforce causes an increase in unemployment. The facts show that just like the amount of labor is not fixed, neither is the size of the economy (fixed pie fallacy) and as more work is done, the economy grows."
